en: There was the Hare, the Snake,
There was the Hen, the Dragon,
There was the Monkey, and the Sheep,
There was the Pig, there was the Dog.
This year is the time he turns twelve.
My foal left by the Magnanimous,
If Semetey is still alive,
This year is the time he turns twelve.
Bereaved Kanykey said:
‘Put aside your sorrow and tend your camels,
Leopard elder, Khan Bakay.
The orphan left by the hero,
When he reaches twelve years of age,
To this very Talas
I will bring him,’ she said.
When fortune turns again for this head of mine,
Is there a night like the Night of Power?
For this head of mine in old age,
Is there a day when Semetey will come?
My honor recovered this year,
My exposed places covered,
All my grief scattered,
My brow opening like the dawn,
Is there a day when Semetey will come?
My child, have you come from the direction of Bukhara?
My child, have you heard news from Bukhara?
If you tell me good news,
I shall agree to what you say.
The orphan has seven hundred camels;
I shall give them as a reward for news of my boy.”
Thus spoke Bakay Khan,
As he asked about Semetey.
Then the boy thought:
“Let me test what Bakay has in mind;
Let me tell him of his boy Semetey.”
Thinking this, Semetey said:
“Brother-in-law, I came from Bukhara.
More than merely coming from there,
I heard the news seething within it.
Manas's son Semetey—
When Kanykey fled there before,
The orphan, Manas's son,
Had an amulet hung about his neck.
He was called Ysmayyl's son
And brought up by his maternal uncle.
His twig was cut,
His rites were performed.
He was made to step over a dog's bowl
And across the edge of a sword.
Kanykey entered Bukhara
And, together with herself, gave her child
To Ysmayyl.
This year your boy Semetey
Proved a glowing ember.
In the mighty city of Bukhara
There was no other such troublemaker.
He imprisoned the wandering dervishes
And beat the mendicants.
The white-turbaned religious masters
And the mullahs studying their lessons—
He thrashed them all
And locked them in their mosque.
When they saw all his mischief,
All the people of Bukhara grew weary.
He proved a glowing ember.
In the mighty city of Bukhara
There was no other such troublemaker.
His religious masters were beaten;
They stabbed the footprints he left
And slandered your only son Semetey.
Temir Khan, the khan of Bukhara,
Was deeply troubled
And shed tears.
‘If this boy hears who his father was,
Will he slaughter my village?
There is no sieve over the people's mouths;
Some witless dog
May tell him.
When my orphan grows angry,
Saying, “You knew I had wandered away;
You kept my lineage hidden,”
He will plunder my valuables
And unleash destruction everywhere.
He will smash my stone-built bazaar,
Slaughter everyone, and take my people
Driving them away to Talas.
He will destroy my possessions
And finish me off completely.’
Fearing the outcome, Temir Khan
Opened the treasury.
Countless treasures and much gold
He scattered, spending them on the people.
He did not simply stand and watch.
When he saw the boy's wrath,
He gathered the peoples of eight khans.
Holding horse races and a feast,
He assembled the people of the world.
When the peoples of eight khans had come,
To those who knew his origins,
He said, ‘Khan Manas's memorial feast’;
To those who knew nothing,
He said, ‘Semetey's celebration.’
Dust rose amid the turmoil;
The ground was filled with teeming people.
Many a mighty warrior came;
Many a mighty lion came.
The horse trainers grew excited.
The mourning woman Kanykey,
Poor soul, took it as an omen:
‘If Taytoru comes in first,
I shall return and see the Kyrgyz;
If Taytoru does not win,
Today I shall die before my appointed time.’
Kanykey, built like a warrior,
Took her lovely, long, thick braid
And bound it tightly atop her head.
The poor soul, fierce and passionate,
Put on a man's clothes.
Concealing that she was a woman,
Leading Taytoru,
She brought him into Bukhara.
When she entered Bukhara
With Taytoru in his sixty-fourth year,
The people of Bukhara crowded around.
All the peoples of eight khans
Marvelled at bereaved Kanykey.
They clamoured their greetings,
Parting sharply into two throngs.
Thus she gained honour.
Kanykey, seeking an omen,
Entered Taytoru in the race.
There were six hundred and forty-three horses
From the peoples of eight khans.
God granted her wish:
Outstripping all six hundred,
Taytoru came galloping in.
Manas's son Semetey,
Not yet knowing about his father,
Raised the battle cry, ‘Manas!’
A courser such as Taytoru
He spurred on with cries of ‘Manas!’
When the boy called out, ‘Manas!’
‘This boy was born greater,’ they said.
The birches wept; the willows wept.
Everyone who looked at the boy wept.
The champion blessed with victory wept.
When the boy called out, ‘Manas!’
The peoples of eight khans all wept.
Even the hard-hearted warrior wept.
All those who wept
Wept, consumed by their own grief.
‘A male child, poor orphan—
If a man leaves one descendant behind,
The decree God has laid down,
The dear soul need never experience.
If a valiant young man
Leaves one descendant behind,
With people saying, “That man's son,”
He does not die after all!’
Taytoru had come first in Bukhara.
The poor orphan left by Manas
The many prizes in Bukhara
He swept up completely.
Bukhara's eighty wrestlers
Said, ‘What of your promise, sir?’
And stood up in a row.
Then the orphan Semetey
Agreed to what they said.
There were a thousand dark camels,
A thousand black mares with white blazes,
Seven houses full of yellow gold,
With rubies and diamonds mixed among it.
The boy became their owner.
Without keeping half a copper coin,
Without setting aside half a mare,
The many prizes in Bukhara,
To the wrestlers, Semetey
Divided them and gave them away.
The people crowded around to watch
And marvelled at the boy:
‘Whom God has truly created—
Truly, he is His servant;
Of poor Manas the mighty warrior,
Truly, he is the son.’
Without speaking openly, they shifted about.
The eight khans traded rumours,
Each one shifting about.
While this was going on,
Temir Khan in Bukhara
Had a proclamation made to his people:
‘My only son shall ascend the throne!’
Upon a gold-patterned carpet
They placed the boy.
Sixty wrestlers lifted him
And, to Bukhara's golden throne,
Carried him all the way.
They seated him on the golden throne;
Saying “Amen!” over the boy,
They raised him up as khan.
With this, in Bukhara
An uproar broke out.
Then Bukhara's khan, Temir Khan,
Was deeply moved;
Tears streamed from his eyes.
When Semetey ascended the throne,
The khan seemed overjoyed.
From the top of the minaret
He roared fiercely,
Summoning the peoples of eight khans:
‘My dear eight khans,
Let your great men come, your elders come;
All you people, come, every one!
I invite you to a solemn feast.
My dear eight khans,
When my boy ascends the throne,
How could I spare my livestock?
Not just my livestock, eight khans—
How could I spare even my life?
My dear eight khans,
This Semetey standing here
Is my spring that feeds a river,
My long-awaited little orphan.
My precious star in heaven,
My silver-fox and otter fur upon my collar,
My long-awaited only child.
Listen, my people: since I became Temir Khan,
Since I acquired the name Temir Khan,
Since I grew to maturity and became a man,
Standing equal to other men's sons,
Since I put on this golden crown of mine
And ruled Bukhara,
I married, established a household and kept livestock,
And supported so many people.
Then my wide world grew narrow:
I yearned for just one child.
When I prayed to God for a child,
I had twelve daughters in succession.
The thirteenth was Kanykey;
The fourteenth, Ysmayyl.
At long last, I had an only son.
Listen to my words, my people:
Ysmayyl's child
Is this Semetey standing here.
When my only son ascends the throne,
How could I begrudge my life?
For this child's feast
I put up a thousand dark camels,
A thousand black mares with white blazes,
And gold weighed out by the pood.
One wrestler stepped out from that side;
One wrestler stepped out from this side.
Hold a wrestling match on foot!
Let the man thrown down go empty-handed;
Let the winner grow rich!
At Semetey's feast,
